newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Ortega tops Aleman in poll of Nicaraguan capital.
newsitem.headline: Ortega tops Aleman in poll of Nicaraguan capital.

text.p: The upward surge in polls by left-wing Nicaraguan presidential candidate Daniel Ortega continued on Sunday, with a poll of Managua residents giving him a narrow lead over right-wing rival Arnold Aleman.
It was the first time Ortega, a former president once given up for dead by political analysts, has led Aleman in a poll. One political analyst said Ortega is now the favourite.
The poll by Nicaraguan firm CINCO S.A. gave Ortega of the Sandinista Front 33.1 percent of the vote and Aleman of the Liberal Alliance 32.1 percent, with 18 percent of those polled undecided.

Some 22 lesser presidential candidates barely scored in the run-up to the October 20 vote. If no candidate receives at least 45 percent of the vote, a second round of voting will be held on an as-yet-undetermined date.
The poll, conducted only in Nicaragua's capital city, showed Ortega topping Aleman in popularity among Managua's low-income and marginalized sectors, while Aleman led among middle-income groups.
The poll surveyed 1,188 people between September 8-16, with a margin of error of 2.8 percent.

"This is a dangerous trend for Aleman since 70 percent of Nicaragua's electorate comes from the low-income and marginalized sectors," poll analyst Raul Obregon told the Nicaraguan newsmagazine Confidencial.
"If nothing changes, if this trend doesn't vary, Ortega looks like the favourite," he said.

The Sandinista Front, with Ortega at the helm, governed Nicaragua from 1979 to 1990, carrying out a Cuban- and Soviet-backed revolution and fighting an eight-year civil war against U.S.-armed Contra rebels that left 25,000 dead.
Ortega, first elected president in 1984, was upset by President Violeta Chamorro in 1990 elections, and has edged back toward the political centre for this year's campaign.
Ortega has undergone a political rebirth, closing the once seemingly unbreachable gap between him and Aleman, the populist former mayor of Managua favoured by business sectors.
Polls consistently show that Ortega's popularity has risen by more than 10 percent since the end of 1995.

Analysts attributed Ortega's rising popularity to discontent with Nicaragua's economic crisis and a well-orchestrated election campaign by the Sandinistas, who still count on a huge network of activists and ownership of a television station and various popular radio stations.
